b1-unit-53.53.1 Gap Year Diaries: big families, sma:
Danny: Welcome back to Gap Year Diaries! Today's topic is population: big cities, big families and small families. With me are Ana and Mrs. Lima.
Mrs. Lima: Hello everyone!
Danny: Mrs. Lima, how many brothers and sisters did you have?
Mrs. Lima: Seven! We lived in a small house above my father's bakery. Eight children and one bathroom!
Ana: And now you have two children.
Mrs. Lima: Yes, and only one grandchild. Times have changed.
Ana: In my family it's the same. My grandmother grew up on a farm with ten brothers and sisters. My mother had two children, me and Paulo. And I have one son.
Danny: Why do you think families are getting smaller?
Ana: In my opinion, it's mainly the cost. Raising a child in São Paulo is expensive, and housing isn't affordable for a lot of young people. Also, women study longer and work more, so many of them decide to have children later.
Mrs. Lima: And people moved to the big cities. In a small apartment, there's no space for eight children!
Danny: Speaking of space... São Paulo is huge. Do you think it will keep growing?
Ana: I think that by the time Leo is my age, the city will have grown even more. And the traffic will probably have gotten worse too.
Mrs. Lima: Or maybe a lot of people will have moved to smaller towns. Many young people work from home now. The big cities will have to cope with that shift.
Danny: So, are you optimistic or pessimistic?
Ana: Optimistic! By twenty-fifty, I hope we'll have found better ways to share water, food and space.
Mrs. Lima: By twenty-fifty, I'll have celebrated my ninetieth birthday. And I'll still be running this hostel!
Danny: And by then I'll have learned perfect Portuguese. I promise!
Ana: Danny, don't make promises you can't keep!
